questions.question: In immersive experience design, which interaction category is mainly used to set up a system, initialize parameters, and choose options or menus?
options: Object manipulation
Environment modeling
Navigation
System control
questions.explanation: System control is the interaction category used for system setup, parameter initialization, and selecting options or menus.

questions.question: How is navigation distinguished from object interaction in immersive experience design?
options: It selects a virtual object and then changes one of its properties.
It creates a virtual scene by converting surfaces into triangular meshes.
It moves the viewpoint from one virtual location to another, mostly without manipulating objects.
It aligns virtual content with a matching real-world region.
questions.explanation: Navigation involves moving from one point in the virtual world to another with a corresponding change in viewpoint, and it mostly does not involve object interaction.

questions.question: In virtual object interaction, how do selection and manipulation differ?
options: Selection sets system options; manipulation specifies virtual objects.
Selection changes object properties; manipulation specifies objects from a virtual set.
Selection specifies objects; manipulation changes properties of an already selected object.
Selection moves the user's viewpoint; manipulation changes object properties.
questions.explanation: Object interaction includes selection for specifying one or more objects and manipulation for changing the properties of selected objects.

questions.question: Which variable can determine which object-selection technique is suitable, alongside target distance and direction?
options: The physical surface property of the target object
The triangular mesh complexity of the target object
The matched-zone alignment of the target with the real world
The density of objects around the target object
questions.explanation: Selection performance is influenced by variables such as target distance, direction, size, density around the target, and the number of targets.

questions.question: What special consideration applies to selecting a fully occluded virtual object?
options: It requires no specialized technique because occlusion is irrelevant.
The user must first be made aware that the object is present.
It is usually the majority case in object selection.
It becomes easier than selecting a partially visible object.
questions.explanation: Partly occluded targets are challenging, and fully occluded targets require awareness of their presence before they can be selected.

questions.question: Which option lists two object-selection techniques?
options: Object manipulation and volume-based selection
Pointing-based selection and bimanual selection
Hand manipulation and camera navigation
Navigation and system control
questions.explanation: Object selection techniques include hand selection, pointing-based selection, image plane selection, volume-based selection, and bimanual selection.

questions.question: What characterizes the virtual hand hand-selection technique?
options: A virtual hand remains still when the physical hand moves below a specified minimum velocity
A virtual hand is guided by a ray that selects the first object it intersects
A visible virtual hand follows the physical hand through a one-to-one mapping of motion and orientation
A visible virtual hand changes the virtual arm length to reach distant objects quickly
questions.explanation: The virtual hand technique uses a visible hand as an avatar of the physical hand, tied to it by a one-to-one mapping of motion and orientation.

questions.question: In go-go hand selection, why can selecting a distant small object be imprecise?
options: As distance increases, small physical hand movements are mapped to larger and faster virtual hand movements
The physical and virtual hands maintain a fixed one-to-one mapping at all distances
The virtual hand remains still when the physical hand moves below a specified minimum velocity
The virtual hand moves more slowly when the target object is farther away
questions.explanation: Go-go maps smaller physical movements to larger and faster virtual movements for farther objects, so a small movement can miss or cross a distant small target.

questions.question: How does the prism technique improve on go-go for distant objects?
options: It slows or stops the virtual hand when the physical hand moves below specified velocity thresholds
It bends a virtual ray toward the closest selectable object before selection
It requires the user to position virtual fingers around the object to refine the selection
It keeps the virtual hand moving at full speed even when the physical hand is stopped
questions.explanation: Prism applies scaled-down motion when the physical hand moves slowly and keeps the virtual hand still below a minimum velocity, giving a control benefit not present in go-go.

questions.question: What does intent-driven selection use to refine which object is selected?
options: A one-to-one mapping of physical hand motion to a visible virtual hand
A scaled mapping in which small physical movements move the virtual hand faster
Hand or finger postures that progressively reduce proximity spheres around the target
A ray from the head or eye that selects the first intersected object
questions.explanation: Intent-driven selection uses virtual hand movement and finger postures, often with proximity spheres that shrink as the user gets closer, to refine the selection.

questions.question: In basic pointing-based object selection, how does the user select a virtual object?
options: Choosing the object nearest to the controller regardless of the ray
Extending a visible ray and triggering the controller to select the first intersected object
Moving a virtual hand until it directly touches the object
Pointing at an object and holding it until it automatically selects
questions.explanation: Pointing-based selection works by extending a visible ray into the virtual world and using a controller trigger to select the first object intersected by that ray.

questions.question: How can the pointing ray be moved without the user using a hand?
options: By moving the body in place
By moving the head or changing the eye gaze
By pressing a selection button on a wristband
By moving a hand-held controller
questions.explanation: Pointing can be done with head movement from a head-mounted display or with eye-gaze tracking, both without hand use.

questions.question: Why can selecting a small distant object be difficult in ray casting?
options: It requires precise pointing, especially when other objects surround it
It requires the ray to automatically bend toward the object
It requires a depth marker to be placed at the object
It requires the user to physically reach the object
questions.explanation: In ray casting, the ray must be pointed precisely, and the difficulty increases when a small object is surrounded by other objects.

questions.question: How does bend cast help a user select an object?
options: It bends the ray toward the closest selectable object
It selects the largest object intersected by the ray
It extends the ray only to a fixed distance
It uses a depth marker to choose among objects
questions.explanation: Bend cast improves basic ray casting by bending the ray toward the closest selectable object, so the user does not need to point as precisely.

questions.question: What does the depth ray technique add to basic ray casting?
options: An eye-gaze estimate that replaces the pointing ray
A user-controlled depth marker that selects the intersected object closest to the marker
A circular arc that visually bends the ray
A timer that selects the first highlighted object
questions.explanation: Depth ray uses a user-controlled depth marker to disambiguate multiple intersected objects and select the intersected object closest to the marker.

questions.question: Which description best matches image-plane selection?
options: A 3D selection made by shaping a box around the object with both hands
A selection made by pointing a ray and choosing the first intersected object
A 2D selection made by aligning an object with a hand between the eye and the object
A selection made by casting a cone and choosing the objects inside it
questions.explanation: Image-plane selection is a 2D selection on a view plane. The user holds a hand or finger between the eye and the object and signals when the object lines up with the hand and eye.

questions.question: How does volumetric selection extend image-plane selection?
options: By letting the user select the first object intersected by a virtual ray
By letting the user select an object on a 2D view plane
By letting the user select an object directly under a single finger
By letting the user select a 3D region so objects inside it are selected
questions.explanation: Volumetric selection allows selection of a 3D region in virtual space, with objects within that region selected. The region can be a box, sphere, or cone.

questions.question: What does the cone casting flashlight technique do?
options: It casts a sphere onto the nearest intersected surface and selects objects within the sphere
It casts a cone to a distance and selects the objects within the cone
It holds a hand between the eye and the object until they line up
It uses both hands to shape and reduce a box around a 3D region
questions.explanation: The cone casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection method that extends ray casting by casting a cone and selecting objects inside that cone.

questions.question: What is two-handed box selection?
options: A technique in which a sphere is cast onto a surface and objects inside the sphere are selected
A technique in which a hand is held between the eye and an object to align it
A technique in which a cone is cast to a distance and objects inside the cone are selected
A bimanual technique in which both hands position, orient, and shape a box to select a 3D region
questions.explanation: Two-handed box selection uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube, and progressively reduces it to select a specified 3D region.

questions.question: When is a volumetric selection technique less effective for selecting smaller objects?
options: When the pointing ray intersects only a single object
When the virtual environment is complex and contains many objects
When the user is selecting on a two-dimensional view plane
When the target object is small, well-defined, and isolated
questions.explanation: Volumetric selection is most useful for small, well-defined isolated objects in a less complex virtual environment. Selecting smaller objects becomes problematic when the environment is complex with many objects.

questions.question: In XR interaction, object manipulation mainly refers to what?
options: Tracking the user's sense organs to update a VR system's input
Estimating the viewer's pose relative to an anchor in the real world
Selecting an object by framing it with the hands in a 2D image plane
Changing an object's properties, such as position, orientation, scale, or texture, after it is selected
questions.explanation: Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object.

questions.question: Which of the following is an object manipulation technique?
options: Volumetric selection
Sense-organ tracking
Image plane selection
Bimanual manipulation
questions.explanation: Manipulation techniques include hand manipulation, indirect manipulation, bimanual manipulation, and integrated hybrid manipulation.

questions.question: What is the core idea behind hand manipulation?
options: Using a virtual hand to manipulate objects
Applying operations to an object's local coordinate system
Framing an object with the hands in a 2D image plane
Using a cone to select objects within a 3D region
questions.explanation: Hand manipulation extends the virtual hand idea and uses a virtual hand to manipulate objects.

questions.question: Which statement is true about hand manipulation?
options: It is a two-dimensional selection technique performed on a view plane
It requires casting a cone to select multiple objects in 3D space
It follows hand selection and can use smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controller-based interaction
It is the least intuitive way of manipulating objects
questions.explanation: Hand manipulation follows hand selection and is implemented using smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controller-based interaction, and it is the most intuitive way of manipulating objects.

questions.question: What is a potential drawback of hand manipulation?
options: It requires registering virtual content to a real-world anchor
It may require more computational power or relatively costly specialized devices
It requires casting a cone instead of a ray for selection
It requires a stationary transmitter that produces a magnetic field
questions.explanation: Hand manipulation requires somewhat more computational power or specialized devices, which may be relatively costly.

questions.question: In indirect object manipulation, how does a user affect a virtual object?
options: By manipulating other objects that are mapped to the virtual object
By grasping the virtual object with a virtual hand
By selecting the object on a view plane from a distance
By moving two handheld controllers symmetrically around an imaginary axis
questions.explanation: Indirect manipulation does not use the physical hand directly on the virtual object; instead, the user manipulates other mapped objects, and those objects manipulate the virtual object.

questions.question: What is a three-dimensional widget used for object manipulation?
options: A virtual hand used to grasp virtual objects
A physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set
A control placed directly in the 3D scene with the virtual object
A miniature handheld model of the entire virtual environment
questions.explanation: A 3D widget is a simple indirect manipulation control placed in the 3D scene, and manipulating it manipulates the associated virtual object.

questions.question: Why may multiple three-dimensional widgets be needed to manipulate one virtual object?
options: Each widget requires synchronous movement of both hands
Each widget is a miniature handheld model of the scene
Each widget typically controls only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom
Each widget represents the entire virtual environment
questions.explanation: A single 3D widget may not be sufficient to manipulate all properties of an object, so specified sets of degrees of freedom are handled by individual widgets.

questions.question: How does world in miniature allow manipulation of a distant virtual object?
options: The user manipulates the distant object's representation in the miniature model
The user grasps the distant object with a virtual hand
The user first selects the distant object in the virtual environment
The user selects the object on a view plane from a distance
questions.explanation: World in miniature represents all objects in the virtual world, so a distant object can be manipulated through its miniature representation without first selecting the distant object.

questions.question: Why is implementing world in miniature not very practical for large and complex virtual environments?
options: The miniature model can show only objects within the user's reach
Creating a miniature model for such environments is very difficult
The miniature model requires synchronous movement of both hands
The user must select each distant object before manipulating it
questions.explanation: World in miniature is not very practical for large and complex environments because creating the required miniature model is very difficult.

questions.question: In bimanual manipulation, what does synchronous hand movement mean?
options: Only one hand controls the object
The hands must be placed symmetrically
The hands do not need to move simultaneously
Both hands move together
questions.explanation: Synchronous bimanual manipulation means both hands move together, while asynchronous means the hands do not need to move simultaneously.

questions.question: Which bimanual manipulation technique uses two six-degree-of-freedom handheld controllers placed symmetrically around an imaginary axis?
options: World in miniature
HOMER
The spindle technique
Spindle plus wheel
questions.explanation: The spindle technique is a symmetric synchronous bimanual technique that uses two six-degree-of-freedom handheld controllers placed symmetrically around an imaginary axis.

questions.question: In the spindle technique, what can moving both hands in unison do to a virtual object?
options: Move it using a single hand
Move and rotate it simultaneously
Rotate it, but not move it
Move it, but not rotate it
questions.explanation: In the spindle technique, moving both hands in unison can move a virtual world object, and the technique can also rotate the object simultaneously.

questions.question: Why can the spindle technique be difficult to use efficiently?
options: It requires moving only one handheld controller
It requires switching between selection and manipulation modes
It requires asymmetric hand placement around an imaginary axis
It requires synchronous hand movement that needs practice
questions.explanation: The spindle technique can be hard to use because it requires synchronous hand movement while interacting in a virtual world, which needs a lot of practice to use efficiently.

questions.question: How does spindle plus wheel differ from the spindle technique?
options: It is asymmetric but synchronous, with hands moved together without symmetric placement
It is symmetric but synchronous, with hands placed symmetrically
It is asymmetric but asynchronous, so the hands need not move together
It is symmetric but asynchronous, so the hands need not move together
questions.explanation: Spindle plus wheel is an asymmetric but synchronous extension of the spindle technique: both hands move together, but they do not need to be placed symmetrically around an imaginary axis.

questions.question: How do integrated hybrid manipulation techniques manage the transition between selecting and manipulating virtual objects?
options: They require the user to send an explicit signal before each transition between modes.
They switch automatically from selection to manipulation and back without an explicit user signal.
They keep selection and manipulation as permanently separate, non-switching modes.
They switch back to selection only when the virtual hand leaves the selected object.
questions.explanation: Integrated hybrid manipulation techniques automatically switch from selection to manipulation after selection and switch back after manipulation, without an explicit user signal.

questions.question: What two interaction methods are integrated in HOMER?
options: Hand manipulation and system control.
Ray-casting selection and hand manipulation.
Ray-casting selection and navigation.
Indirect manipulation and bimanual manipulation.
questions.explanation: HOMER integrates ray casting, a pointing-based selection method, with hand manipulation so that selection and manipulation are not performed separately.

questions.question: In HOMER, when the selected ray intersects the desired object, what happens next?
options: The user's virtual hand automatically moves to the object and attaches to it.
The object automatically moves to the user's virtual hand.
The ray automatically attaches to the object.
The virtual hand remains in its original position.
questions.explanation: In HOMER, the virtual hand moves automatically to the intersected object and attaches to it, rather than the ray being attached to the object.

questions.question: After the virtual hand attaches to an object in HOMER, what does the user do with the object?
options: The user performs system control with familiar computer controls.
The user changes its position and orientation through hand manipulation.
The user controls the scene through a 3D widget.
The user navigates to another point in the virtual world.
questions.explanation: After the virtual hand attaches to the object, HOMER switches to manipulation mode, allowing the user to change the object's position and orientation through hand manipulation.

questions.question: What ends the manipulation phase in HOMER?
options: The object reaches a predefined position.
The ray no longer intersects the selected object.
The user indicates that the job is done with a trigger or a specific hand gesture.
The virtual hand stops moving for a set period.
questions.explanation: Manipulation ends when the user indicates completion through a trigger or a specific hand gesture, after which the virtual hand returns to its original position.

activities.title: Order the steps of HOMER object manipulation

items.title: Order the steps of HOMER object manipulation
steps: The user selects an object with ray casting
The ray intersects the desired object
The virtual hand moves to the object
The virtual hand attaches to the object

questions.question: Why can augmented reality systems use regular interaction techniques?
options: Because the user's senses are not blocked
Because the user is completely cut off from the real world
Because the user's senses are blocked
Because the interaction requires bimanual synchronized movement
questions.explanation: Augmented reality systems allow regular interaction techniques to be used with the virtual augmentation of the real world because the user's senses are not blocked.

questions.question: Why do immersive environments need improved interaction techniques?
options: Because they block the user's senses and cut the user off from the real world
Because they depend only on ordinary computer-system controls
Because they leave the user's real-world senses fully available
Because they allow regular interaction with the real-world augmentation
questions.explanation: Immersive environments block the user's senses and cut the user off from the real world in the ideal case, so improved interaction techniques are needed for a better immersive experience.

questions.question: Which pair of interaction techniques is typically used in immersive environments and related to virtual objects?
options: Object selection and navigation
Navigation and system control
Object manipulation and system control
Object selection and object manipulation
questions.explanation: Object selection and object manipulation are the two interaction techniques, typically used in immersive environments, that are related to virtual objects.

questions.question: What is the purpose of navigation techniques?
options: Changing settings on a computer system
Selecting virtual objects with a pointing ray
Matching virtual content with real-world surfaces
Moving from one point to another in a virtual world
questions.explanation: Navigation techniques are interaction techniques for moving from one point to another in a virtual world.

questions.question: What does system control interaction primarily rely on?
options: Techniques for manipulating virtual objects with both hands
Improved techniques required for fully immersive environments
Regular interaction techniques familiar from ordinary computer systems
Techniques for moving between locations in a virtual world
questions.explanation: System control interaction primarily relies on regular interaction techniques that are familiar when dealing with any computer system.

Object interaction
Navigation

items.reason: Object interaction, navigation, and system control are the three broad categories of interaction, while selection is a type of object interaction.

Prism technique
Virtual hand technique
Ray casting technique
items.reason: Virtual hand, go-go, and prism are hand selection techniques, while ray casting is a pointing-based selection technique.

Cone casting technique
Sticky finger technique
Head crusher technique
items.reason: Head crusher, sticky finger, and lifting palm are image plane selection techniques, while cone casting is a volumetric selection technique.

questions.question: In immersive interaction design, why might head pointing or eye-gaze pointing be useful for selecting virtual objects when hand tracking is unavailable?
questions.reference_answer: Pointing-based selection can be done by hand pointing, head pointing with a head-mounted display, or eye-gaze pointing with an eye tracker. A virtual ray can be attached to the virtual hand, head position, or eye gaze, with head position or eye gaze used when hand tracking is unavailable.

questions.question: How do the go-go and prism techniques change virtual hand selection for distant objects, and why might prism still be preferable to go-go?
questions.reference_answer: A direct virtual hand can require a long duration of physical hand movement to reach distant objects, so the go-go technique changes the virtual arm length and maps smaller physical hand movements to faster virtual hand movement. Prism applies scaled-down motion when the physical hand moves below a specified speed and leaves the virtual hand still when the physical hand is slower than a specified minimum speed. Prism can therefore be a better solution for distant objects because the virtual hand slows or stops when the physical hand slows or stops, although it does not use a one-to-one mapping, which may be counterintuitive.

questions.question: Why can selecting small or tightly grouped objects be difficult in both ray casting and volumetric selection, even though they use different selection geometries?
questions.reference_answer: Ray casting requires precise pointing of a virtual ray, so selecting small distant objects is difficult, especially when the small object is surrounded by other objects. The cone casting flashlight technique is volumetric and selects the objects within a cone, so selecting smaller or tightly grouped objects can be difficult. Volumetric selection is most useful for small or well-defined isolated objects in a less complex virtual environment and becomes problematic when the environment is complex with many objects.

questions.question: Why might a single three-dimensional widget not be enough to fully manipulate a virtual object, and how does that follow from the idea of degrees of freedom?
questions.reference_answer: Degrees of freedom describe the different ways an object can move in space, and in three-dimensional space an object can have six degrees of freedom: three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes and three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch. A three-dimensional widget is typically responsible only for a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom. Therefore, specified sets of degrees of freedom are manipulated using individual widgets rather than one widget for all properties.
